concepts: attempt; endeavor; effort; trial; test; practice; experiment; examination; tasting; sample; quality; attack; experience
notes: One noun occurrence in Chapter 1, 'their youthful assay of the ancient arts', where young feylings demonstrate developing magical craft. Primary OED match III.16, 'a first tentative effort, in learning or practice' (?1570–1677, obsolete); secondary III.13, attempt or endeavour (c1386 onward, archaic). OED assay n. first attested 1330 (ME), French borrowing via assai, ultimately Latin exagium; essay displaced most general senses, while metal and later biological assay continue. Historical senses also encompass trial, testing, experiment, experience, best effort, tasting, inspection, a sample, assault and standard of quality; see Evidence row 96 for sense distinctions. The idiom 'at all assays' (at every trial or occasion; alternatively armed and ready) is OED-attested but does not occur in the manuscript and is not separately entered. Era range ME to PDE reflects full noun entry including 1961 bioassay, not continued use of obsolete III.16. Author-assigned Tier 4.

concepts: go; travel; journey; move; proceed; turn; change; return; depart; direct; transform; follow a course
notes: 19 manuscript uses of the verb (7 wend, 12 wended), plus one nominalized 'wending' in Chapter 13 for later noun-specific OED review. All eight verb-using chapters: 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11. Principal OED wend v.1 senses: II.8.b physical movement or journey; II.8.c thoughts, musings, paths or courses proceeding in a direction; II.8.d transitive route/way, especially 'wend one's way'. Secondary comparison I.6.a for 'wended back into the lore that made her' (figurative return; original sense obsolete). 'Wended the knotted wild' with wilderness as direct object is not independently confirmed by supplied OED quotations. Other senses in the same OED verb entry include turning, redirecting one's mind, changing or transforming, nautical tacking, departure and obsolete extended meanings; see Evidence #97 for detailed classification. Germanic inheritance; 'went' from wend became past tense of go; newer 'wended' developed for wend. OE through PDE evidenced in OED, which describes the modern verb as somewhat literary. Tier 4 explicitly chosen by User. No separate idiom or grammar record added.

concepts: journey; travel; movement; wandering; progress; turn; change; nautical tacking; meandering
notes: One noun use, Chapter 13: 'They were some few days beyond the usual wending', where preceding context describes difficult southward travel slowed by mud and ice. Primary OED match sense 3 'a journey' (1340–1500, obsolete), potentially the usual journey's expected duration; related sense 2.a 'the act of going or wandering' (c1330–, somewhat literary). The noun is independently recorded in OED from Old English (sense 1.a turning/change), through modern quotation evidence for 2.a and 2.b (the winding course of a river or road). Other noun sense 1.b denotes nautical turning. The exact phrasing 'the usual wending' has not been independently verified as a historical formula. OED Meaning & use supplied; noun Factsheet and Etymology not supplied. Separate dictionary entry from wend v.1, Evidence and Register #97. Tier 4 expressly assigned by User.

concepts: knowledge; learning; instruction; teaching; doctrine; counsel; advice; tradition; legends; beliefs; erudition; science; information; story
notes: Six noun occurrences, no plurals: Ch. 1 'wended back into the lore that made her' and 'the telling of the lore and laurelled deeds'; Ch. 2 'its wont of spellcraft and lore'; Ch. 4 'vanished lore'; Ch. 5 'the prophecies and deep lore of the Elder Fire' and 'Feifýren lore and legend'. Main OED lore n.1 match sense 5.a learned knowledge and traditional facts, stories and beliefs (a1225–); sense 2.a religious or moral doctrine is a potential secondary match for Elder Fire. Other senses include instruction/lesson (1), plural precepts (2.b), creed (2.c), rule of conduct (2.d), advice or counsel (3), spoken story/information (4) and a body of knowledge or science (5.b); see Evidence 99. Inherited Germanic, Old English lār, cognate with Old Saxon lêra, Old High German lêra; see learn. First evidence OE, latest dated OED quote supplied 1901 (LMdE), although OED also reports modern use; era_range reflects last dated quotation. No separate manuscript idiom identified. Tier 4 assigned by User.

concepts: dwelling; abode; village; hamlet; settlement; farm; dairy farm; enclosure
notes: Two manuscript noun uses, both plural 'wykes' in the phrase 'woad wykes': Chapter 1 'They bided amidst the heather and bilberry out on Seer’s Moor, in their woad wykes'; Chapter 3 'Fast-bound and burdened, he rode through mist and woad wykes'. OED dictionary headword is wick n.2 (distinct from lamp-wick); register headword retains author's plural 'wykes'. Strongest possible OED matches: sense 1 abode/dwelling (OE–1300, obsolete) and sense 2 town/village/hamlet (OE onward, obsolete or dialect); passage does not determine whether individual dwellings or small settlements. Senses 3 farm/dairy farm (now local) and 4 enclosed ground or close (obsolete and local) are documented but not established by the scene.
